Oblivious Points on Translation SurfacesThanks: *corresponding author

Ian Adelstein*, Krish Desai, Anthony Ji, Grace Zdeblick Address: Department of Mathematics, Yale University, 10 Hillhouse Ave, New Haven, CT 06511
Abstract.

An oblivious point on a translation surface is a point with no closed geodesic passing through it. Nguyen, Pan, and Su [1] showed that there are at most finitely many oblivious points on any given translation surface and constructed a family of surfaces with exactly one oblivious point. We construct new families of translation surfaces with arbitrarily many oblivious points and prove that there is a translation surface in every genus ≥3\geq 3 with an oblivious point.

1. Introduction

Translation surfaces are closely related to polygonal billiards and illumination problems. They are surfaces naturally equipped with a flat metric away from a finite set of singularities called cone points. Due to the flat metric, geodesics on these surfaces are straight lines. Closed geodesics are geodesics which close up on themselves smoothly. Nguyen, Pan, and Su [1] investigate the relationship between regular (non-cone) points and closed geodesics. They prove on any translation surface, that the set of regular points not contained in a closed geodesic is finite. Let us call these points oblivious points.

Definition 1.1.

An oblivious point is a regular point on a translation surface through which there are no simple closed geodesics.

Theorem 1.2 ([1], Theorem 1).

The set of oblivious points on a translation surface is finite.

Additionally, they give a construction for a family of surfaces with exactly one oblivious point. A natural question to ask is whether it is possible to find translation surfaces with any number of oblivious points. One may also study the genus of surfaces with oblivious points. In this paper, we demonstrate the following results:

Theorem 1.3.

For every n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} there is a translation surface with exactly nn oblivious points.

Theorem 1.4.

There exist translation surfaces in every genus g≥3g\geq 3 admitting an oblivious point.

It is known that translation surfaces with genus g<3g<3 do not admit oblivious points [1, 2], so in this sense Theorem 1.4 is optimal.

The paper proceeds as follows: In Section 2 a standard background on translation surfaces is presented. In Section 3 the behaviour of oblivious points under translation covering maps is studied. In Section 4 we use the covering technology developed, together with a slit construction and an existence result from [1] to prove Theorem 1.3. We also show how these techniques can be used to produce a translation surface admitting an oblivious point in every genus g≥4g\geq 4. In Section 5 we focus our attention on square-tiled surfaces, and introduce a new construction that allows us to produce translation surfaces admitting an oblivious point in every genus g≥3g\geq 3, completing the proof of Theorem 1.4. This construction also yields translation surfaces admitting nn oblivious points for every n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, thus providing an alternate proof of Theorem 1.3. Finally, in Section 6 we prove results about which square-tiled translation surfaces admit oblivious points.

2. Background

This section includes much of the background necessary to state and prove our main results.

2.1. Translation Surfaces

A translation surface is a collection of polygons in the plane with parallel sides identified by complex translation z↦z+c∈ℂ,z\mapsto z+c\in\mathbb{C}, up to cut and paste. When one identifies sides by translation, certain singular points of concentrated curvature, called cone points, do not have a total angle of 2​π2\pi around them. The angles around these cone points, called cone angles, are integer multiples of 2​π2\pi. A square–tiled surface (STS) is a translation surface of which every polygon is a square.

The genus of a surface can be calculated using only the cone angles through the following theorem.

Theorem 2.1 (Combinatorial Gauss–Bonnet).

Consider a translation surface with cone points pip_{i} and corresponding cone angles αi\alpha_{i}. Define the cone angle excess at each point as ki=αi−2​π2​πk_{i}=\frac{\alpha_{i}-2\pi}{2\pi}. Then

∑iki=2​g−2\sum_{i}k_{i}=2g-2

where gg is the genus of the surface.

Using the same definition for the kik_{i}, surfaces of the same genus may be further partitioned into strata. If XX is a translation surface with cone angle excesses {k1,k2,⋯,kn}\{k_{1},k_{2},\cdots,k_{n}\}, then the surface is in the stratum denoted ℋ⁡(k1,k2,⋯,kn)\mathcal{H}(k_{1},k_{2},\cdots,k_{n}).

2.2. G​L2​(ℝ)GL_{2}(\mathbb{R}) and Veech Group Action

The natural action of the group G​L2​(ℝ)GL_{2}(\mathbb{R}) on a stratum of translation surface is obtained by G​L2​(ℝ)GL_{2}(\mathbb{R}) acting on the polygonal representation of the surface in ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2}.

One might seek to study the induced action of this group on points and geodesics on a translation surface. However, such an action is not quite induced on points and geodesics on the surface, because the cut and paste action described above can identify points on a translation surface with a non-trivial translation automorphism group. Rather, this action is on equivalence classes of points and geodesics modulo this group, rather than directly on points. To resolve this ambiguity, one typically passes to a finite cover of the stratum of translation surfaces, and by marking sufficiently many points one can break the equivalence and distinguish the surfaces. Here the action is indeed on points and geodesics. Since the obliviousness of a point commutes with translation automorphisms, in practice, one can pass freely between the the stratum and its finite cover, though precision about this process is indeed required in formal proof.

Proposition 2.2.

Consider translation surface XX in stratum ℋ\mathcal{H} with an oblivious point at xx, and translation automorphism group GG. Let ϕ:ℋ¯→ℋ\phi:\overline{\mathcal{H}}\to\mathcal{H} be a covering map that breaks the ambiguity created by GG by adding marked points. For every g∈G​L2​(ℝ)g\in GL_{2}(\mathbb{R}) if XgX_{g} is an element of then set ϕ​(g⋅ϕ−1​(X)),\phi(g\cdot\phi^{-1}(X)), and xgx_{g} is an element of the set ϕ​(g⋅ϕ−1​(x))\phi(g\cdot\phi^{-1}(x)) the xgx_{g} is oblivious in Xg.X_{g}.

Proof.

Let XX be a translation surface and x∈Xx\in X an oblivious point. By way of contradiction, assume there exists g∈G​L2​(ℝ)g\in GL_{2}(\mathbb{R}) such that y∈ϕ⁡(g⋅ϕ−1​(x))y\in\phi(g\cdot\phi^{-1}(x)) is contained in a closed geodesic γ\gamma. Since G​L2​(ℝ)GL_{2}(\mathbb{R}) is a group, the element gg is invertible. This implies that there is a closed geodesic in ϕ⁡(g−1⋅ϕ−1​(γ))\phi(g^{-1}\cdot\phi^{-1}(\gamma)) through x=ϕ⁡(g−1⋅ϕ−1​(y))x=\phi(g^{-1}\cdot\phi^{-1}(y)). But xx is an oblivious point by assumption, which leads to a contradiction. ∎

One may summarize the above proposition through the slogan, “the G​L2​(ℝ)GL_{2}(\mathbb{R}) image of an oblivious point is oblivious.”

Definition 2.3.

Given a translation surface XX, its Veech group, S​L​(X)SL(X) is the stabiliser subgroup of XX under S​L2​(ℝ).SL_{2}(\mathbb{R}). It comprises those elements of S​L2​(ℝ)SL_{2}(\mathbb{R}) whose action sends XX back to itself up to cut–and–paste.

Corollary 2.4.

As S​L​(X)SL(X) is a subgroup of G​L2​(ℝ)GL_{2}(\mathbb{R}), the orbit of an oblivious point under the Veech group action consists of oblivious points. Let Trans⁡(X)\operatorname{Trans}(X) be the group of translation automorphisms of X.X. Given (a Trans⁡(X)\operatorname{Trans}(X)-orbit of) an oblivious point on a translation surface XX with non-trivial Veech group, additional oblivious points may be obtained by identifying the points in the orbit with points on XX.

2.3. Covers

A cover of a surface XX is a pair (Y,ρ)(Y,\rho) where YY is a closed surface and ρ:Y→X\rho:Y\to X is a surjective local homeomorphism. The degree of a cover (Y,ρ)(Y,\rho) of a surface XX is the cardinality of the fiber of ρ\rho over any regular point x∈Xx\in X,

deg⁡ρ=|{ρ−1​{x}}|.\deg\rho=|\{\rho^{-1}\{x\}\}|.

A branched cover is a cover which ramifies over a finite set; that is, (Y,ρ)(Y,\rho) is a branched cover of a closed surface XX if there exist finite sets of points, branch points B⊆YB\subseteq Y and branching values V⊆XV\subseteq X, such that ρ:Y∖B→X∖V\rho:Y\setminus B\to X\setminus V is a covering map. A translation cover is a cover, branched or otherwise, which preserves translation structure. In a polygonal representation, a translation cover can be represented as multiple copies of a surface with edge identification preserved between copies. In this paper, we explore primarily branched translation covers.

A fully ramified cover is a cover for which each of the branch points has cone angle that exceeds 2​π2\pi. One may note that translation covers are local isometries.

2.4. Semi-Translation Surfaces

Similar to translation surfaces, semi-translation surfaces, also known as half-translation surfaces, are defined as collections of polygons in the plane with sides identified by translations and 180​deg180\deg-rotations (z↦±z+cz\mapsto\pm z+c) up to cut–and–paste. All cone points on a semi-translation surface have cone angles which are integer multiples of π\pi.

The strata for semi-translation surfaces are defined similarly to those for translation surfaces. For a semi-translation surface XX with cone angles αi\alpha_{i}, define li=αi−2​ππl_{i}=\frac{\alpha_{i}-2\pi}{\pi} and say that XX is in 𝒬⁡(l1,l2,…,ln)\mathcal{Q}(l_{1},l_{2},\ldots,l_{n}).

Any given semi-translation surface can be related to a translation surfact through the following construction. The canonical double cover of a semi-translation surface is defined according to Zorich[2]: a semi-translation surface in the stratum 𝒬⁡(l1,…,ln)\mathcal{Q}(l_{1},\ldots,l_{n}) is mapped to a surface in the stratum ℋ⁡(k1,…,km)\mathcal{H}(k_{1},\ldots,k_{m}) where the {ki}\{k_{i}\} are obtained from the {lj}\{l_{j}\} via the following rules:

  1. (1)

    To each even lj>0l_{j}>0, associate the pair {12​lj,12​lj}\{\frac{1}{2}l_{j},\frac{1}{2}l_{j}\} in the {ki}\{k_{i}\}.

  2. (2)

    To each odd lj>0l_{j}>0, associate {lj+1}\{l_{j}+1\} in the {ki}\{k_{i}\}.

  3. (3)

    No kik_{i} is associated for lj=−1l_{j}=-1.

In words, cone angles that are even multiples of π\pi are duplicated in number and cone angles that are odd multiples of π\pi are doubled in angle. As such, the canonical double cover of a semi-translation surface is a translation surface.

As the first existence result for oblivious points Nguyen, Pan, and Su [1] showed that the canonical double cover can be used to construct oblivious points via the following theorem.

Theorem 2.5 ([1], Proposition 3.1).

Let XX be a semi-translation surface with exactly one cone point yy of cone angle π\pi (other cone points with different cone angles are allowed). The canonical double cover of XX has an oblivious point at the pre-image of yy.

Lemma 2.6 ([1], Remark 3.2i).

If XX has the additional property that every regular point is contained in a simple closed geodesic, then the preimage of yy is the unique oblivious point on the canonical double cover of XX.

A visual representation of the canonical double cover of a semi-translation surface can be constructed with the following algorithm. Note that the goal is to eliminate the reflections, i.e. to take sides that had been identified via translation and reflection, and reassign the identification in a way that eliminates the reflection.

  1. (1)

    Mark sides identified by translation with numbers, and sides identified by translation and reflection with opposite-facing arrows.

  2. (2)

    Take two copies of the surface. Sides identified by translation will be associated as originally. Relabel these sides on one copy of the surface to avoid ambiguity. Leave the arrows alone.

  3. (3)

    Rotate one of the copies by 180o180^{\text{o}}.

  4. (4)

    Leave the association of the numbered sides. Associate sides with arrows with their same orientation counterpart; this eliminates any reflection identification.

This construction duplicates cone angles which are even multiples of π\pi and doubles cone angles which are odd multiples of π\pi, following the involution map described above. Thus the canonical double cover of a semi-translation surface is indeed a translations surface.

3. Translation Covers and Geodesics

In this section we give results on the behavior of closed geodesics under translation covers. We will examine the behavior of preimages of points under translation covers and how it affects the obliviousness of a point.

Lemma 3.1.

The preimage of a point in a non-singular closed geodesic under a fully ramified translation cover is contained in a non-singular closed geodesic.

Proof.

Let (X,P)(X,P) be a translation surface with marked points P={p1,p2,⋯,pk}P=\{p_{1},p_{2},\cdots,p_{k}\} and let YY be a branched translation cover of XX with branched covering map ρ\rho, branching points B⊆YB\subseteq Y, and branching values V⊆XV\subseteq X with P⊆VP\subseteq V. Let γ\gamma be a closed non-singular geodesic in X∖VX\setminus V. Let xx be a point in γ\gamma and y∈ρ−1​(x)y\in\rho^{-1}(x). Denote τ\tau to be the connected component of ρ−1​(γ)\rho^{-1}(\gamma) containing yy. Note that τ\tau is a geodesic since ρ\rho is a local isometry and that ρ⁡(τ)=γ\rho(\tau)=\gamma. Then τ\tau is a closed non-singular geodesic in Y∖BY\setminus B. ∎

The above lemma equivalently states that the preimage of a non-oblivious point under a translation cover is not oblivious. We also demonstrate the converse of this in the following lemma.

Lemma 3.2.

The preimage of an oblivious point under a fully ramified translation cover is oblivious.

Proof.

It suffices to prove the equivalent statement that the image of a non-singular closed geodesic under a translation cover is a non-singular closed geodesic. Let (X,P)(X,P) be a translation surface with marked points P={p1,p2,⋯,pk}P=\{p_{1},p_{2},\cdots,p_{k}\}. Let YY be a branched translation cover of XX with ρ\rho the branched covering map with branching points B⊆YB\subseteq Y and branching values V⊆XV\subseteq X with P⊆VP\subseteq V. We have B=ρ−1​(V)B=\rho^{-1}(V) by definition. Suppose γ⊆Y∖B\gamma\subseteq Y\setminus B is a simple, closed, non-singular geodesic (since all points in BB have cone angle 4​π4\pi or greater, we need not consider closed geodesics containing points in BB). Then since ρ\rho is continuous, ρ⁡(γ)\rho(\gamma) is connected as γ\gamma is connected. Hence ρ⁡(γ)\rho(\gamma) is closed. Moreover ρ\rho is a local isometry, thus ρ⁡(γ)\rho(\gamma) is a geodesic. Now suppose ρ⁡(γ)\rho(\gamma) is singular. Then by assumption ρ⁡(γ)\rho(\gamma) passes through a point in VV. Since γ∩B=∅\gamma\cap B=\emptyset this is impossible. Thus ρ⁡(γ)\rho(\gamma) is non-singular. ∎

We use these lemmas to better understand the relationship between oblivious points and regularly tiled polygonal surfaces.

Lemma 3.3.

Let XX be a translation surface tiled by a regular polygon. Then any oblivious point of XX must be a vertex point.

While this lemma could be shown by considering periodic points on the regular nn–gon, here we provide an elementary proof to show that all non-vertex points are contained in some cylinder.

Proof.

Suppose XX is tiled by a regular nn–gon. We consider two cases.
Case 1: If nn is even, XX is a branched translation cover of the regular nn–gon, whose opposite sides are identified, with the vertices of the nn–gon as the branching values of the translation cover. Any non-vertex point is the preimage of a non-vertex point in the base nn–gon. We show that just three families of cylinders contain all non-vertex points in the base nn-gon.

For simplicity, consider the representation of the nn–gon in the Cartesian plane where the center of the polygon is at the origin and a pair of opposite vertices are on the yy–axis. Pick one of the edges adjacent to a vertex on the yy–axis and consider the cylinder perpendicular to this edge together with all parallel cylinders. The blue lines in Figures 4 and 4 illustrate the only points not contained in this family of cylinders. Now pick the other pair of edges adjacent to the yy–axis and consider its associated family of cylinders. The red lines in Figures 4 and 4 illustrate the only points not contained in this family of cylinders.

For each xx value the blue (alternatively, red) lines contain either one non-vertex point or two vertex points. By the reflection symmetry about the xx–axis we have that these colored lines intersect only at vertex points and along the xx–axis (for the case of n=4n=4, the intersections are only on vertex points). We need only show that these xx–axis intersections are contained in some third family of cylinders.

If n=4​N+2,N∈ℕ,n=4N+2,N\in\mathbb{N}, there is a pair of edges perpendicular to the xx–axis and the xx–axis intersections are contained in the associated cylinder. If n=4​N,N∈ℕ,n=4N,N\in\mathbb{N}, the nn–gon has two vertices on the xx–axis, and the xx–axis intersections are contained in the cylinder associated to one of the edges adjacent to a vertex on the xx–axis. These cylinders are shown in green in Figures 4 and 4. Thus, every non-vertex point is contained in some closed geodesic.

Case 2: If nn is odd, XX is a branched translation cover of the doubled regular nn–gon. The doubled regular nn–gon is a presentation of such a surface in ℝ2\mathbb{R}^{2} with two regular nn–gons with one shared (or “glued”) side, and the parallel edges identified. We show that any non-vertex point in the base doubled regular nn–gon is contained in just two families of cylinders.

Take any pair of associated parallel edges and consider the cylinder decomposition parallel to the lines which connect the identified vertices on this pair of edges. The only non-vertex points not contained this family of cylinders are shown by the blue lines in Figure 4. Now consider an edge which shares a vertex with the first pair of edges and is not the “glued” side of the doubled nn–gon, as well as its associated parallel edge. Again, consider the cylinder decomposition parallel to the lines which connect the identified vertices on this pair of edges. By the choice of using an adjacent edge, the boundaries of this family of cylinders, shown in red in Figure 4, intersect with the boundaries from the first family of cylinders only at vertex points. Thus, every non-vertex point is contained in a cylinder from one of these two sets of cylinders.

By Lemma 3.1 we conclude that only vertex points may be oblivious. ∎

Proposition 3.4.

Any translation surface tiled by a regular polygon other than a triangle, square, or hexagon cannot admit an oblivious point.

Proof.

Suppose XX is a translation surface tiled by a regular nn-gon. The angle at each vertex of a regular nn-gon is (n−2)​πn\frac{(n-2)\pi}{n}. Thus, at any vertex point on XX, the angle must be a multiple of (n−2)​πn\frac{(n-2)\pi}{n}. However, for n≠3,4,6n\neq 3,4,6, (n−2)​πn\frac{(n-2)\pi}{n} does not divide 2​π2\pi. Therefore no vertex point on XX is a regular point and by Lemma 3.3 we see that XX cannot admit an oblivious point. ∎

Remark 3.5.

Any translation surface tiled by equilateral triangles or regular hexagons is in the G​L2​(ℝ){GL}_{2}(\mathbb{R}) orbit of a square tiled surface and thus is also arithmetic. Proposition 3.4 therefore implies that any surface tiled by a regular polygon which contains an oblivious point must be arithmetic. When investigating oblivious points on translation surfaces tiled by regular polygons, we therefore need only consider square tiled surfaces.

4. Connected Translation Surfaces via Slits

Nguyen, Pan, and Su [1, Example 1] construct a translation surface with exactly one oblivious point. One may combine this result with Lemma 3.2 to get a surface with nn oblivious points as follows. Let XX be a translation surface with exactly one oblivious point xx. By Lemma 3.2, for any degree nn translation cover of XX, the preimages of xx are all oblivious. In a degree nn cover, there are nn preimages to any regular point, so a degree nn translation cover has nn preimages of xx. For the trivial n−n- translation cover of nn disconnected copies of XX, this covering space would have nn oblivious points. This produces a disconnected translation surface with nn oblivious points, a somewhat trivial proof of our Theorem 1.3.

However, one would prefer to consider connected translation surfaces, and we extend this result to connected translation surfaces. One may build a connected surface with nn oblivious points simply by taking unbranched translation nn–covers of the surface with one oblivious point demonstrated in [1]. However, by computing the Euler characteristic of these nn–covers, one may observe that one cannot obtain a surface of every genus through this process. In order to provide a fresh construction of connected translation surfaces with nn oblivious points for every positive integer n,n, and connected translation surfaces in every genus g∈ℕ,g\in\mathbb{N}, we first introduce the notion of a slit.

Construction 4.1 (Slits).

Given two disconnected translation surfaces, begin by choosing equal length embedded parallel straight line segments on each surface. Slit the surfaces at these segments, then glue so that the left side of one segment is identified with the right side of the other segment. The result is a connected translation surface with two additional cone points.

Example 4.2.

Given two disconnected tori, as in Figure 5, cut each torus along the parallel segments and glue according to the diagram. Geodesics entering the slit on one surface emerge from the associated slit on the other surface with the same trajectory as shown. In this example the two endpoints of the segment (whose copies are identified under the gluing) become a pair of cone points each with angle excess 2​π2\pi.

This slit construction (together with the existence result from [1, Example 1]) is now used to prove the Theorem 1.3:

Proof of Theorem 1.3.

Let XX be a translation surface with exactly one oblivious point, xx. Label nn disconnected copies of XX as X1,X2,…,XnX_{1},X_{2},\ldots,X_{n}. Choose a closed geodesic γ\gamma on XX that does not contain any cone points or the oblivious point xx. Let yy and zz be any two points on γ\gamma and choose one segment of γ\gamma with endpoints yy and zz. Call this segment EE.

Define yiy_{i} and ziz_{i} on XiX_{i} to be the preimages of yy and zz under the trivial disjoint degree nn covering map from ⋃i=1nXi\bigcup\limits_{i=1}^{n}X_{i} to XX, and similarly define EiE_{i} as the preimage of edge EE. Connect the XiX_{i} by “slitting” them together at the edges EiE_{i}.

Associate slits such that each edge EiE_{i} leads into the edge Ei+1​(m​o​d​n)E_{i+1(mod~n)} (or any permutation of associating the edges which is an nn-cycle). When traversing from EiE_{i} to Ei+1E_{i+1}, a geodesic emerges on Xi+1X_{i+1} in the equivalent position that it would have continued on XiX_{i} were the edges not associated. Under this association the identified yiy_{i} and ziz_{i} each become cone points of angle 2​π​n2\pi n. One has therefore connected the disjoint XiX_{i}, and this connected space is now a degree nn connected translation cover for XX. By Lemma 3.2, the nn preimages of xx are oblivious. ∎

Theorem 4.3.

For every g≥4g\geq 4 there exists a surface YY of genus gg with an oblivious point on it.

Proof.

Masur and Smillie [3, Theorem 2(c)] state that every stratum of semitranslation surfaces except for 𝒬⁡(4),𝒬⁡(3,1),𝒬⁡(1,−1)\mathcal{Q}(4),\mathcal{Q}(3,1),\mathcal{Q}(1,-1) and 𝒬⁡(0)\mathcal{Q}(0) is non-empty.

Case I: Even genus ≥4\geq 4

In particular, for every m∈ℕm\in\mathbb{N} the stratum 𝒬⁡(−1,4​m+1)\mathcal{Q}(-1,4m+1) is nonempty. For every X∈𝒬⁡(−1,4​m+1)X\in\mathcal{Q}(-1,4m+1), let YY be the canonical double cover of XX. Since XX has a single π\pi cone point, by Theorem 2.5, YY contains an oblivious point. By Kontsevich and Zorich [4, Lemma 1] Y∈ℋ⁡(4​m+2)Y\in\mathcal{H}(4m+2). By combinatorial Gauss–Bonnet, YY is a surface of genus 2​m+22m+2.

Case II: Odd genus ≥5\geq 5

By the same theorem of Masur and Smillie, for every m∈ℕm\in\mathbb{N} the stratum 𝒬⁡(−1,1,1,4​n−1)\mathcal{Q}(-1,1,1,4n-1) is nonempty. For every X∈𝒬⁡(−1,1,1,4​m−1)X\in\mathcal{Q}(-1,1,1,4m-1), let YY be the canonical double cover of XX. Since XX has a single π\pi cone point, by Theorem 2.5, YY contains an oblivious point. By Kontsevich and Zorich [4, Lemma 1], Y∈ℋ⁡(2,2,4​m)Y\in\mathcal{H}(2,2,4m). By combinatorial Gauss–Bonnet, YY is a surface of genus 2​m+32m+3. ∎

Proposition 4.4.

There are no surfaces with an oblivious point in genera 1 and 2.

Proof.

Kontsevich and Zorich [4, Theorem 2] state that every stratum in genus 1 and 2 is connected and coincides with its hyperelliptic component.Nygyen, Pan and Su [1, Theorem 3] state that no surface in the hyperelliptic component of any stratum admits an oblivious point. Hence no surface of genus 1 or 2 contains an oblivious point ∎

Remark 4.5.

No genus 3 surface containing an oblivious point can be constructed through Theorem 2.5. The argument in Theorem 4.3 fails in genus 3. Even though the relevant stratum, 𝒬⁡(1,1,−1,−1)\mathcal{Q}(1,1,-1,-1), is non-empty, this stratum fails the hypotheses of Theorem 2.5 as it admits two cone points of cone angle π\pi.

Table 1 lists all possible strata of translation surfaces in genus 3, and the strata of semitranslation surfaces they can double cover. Since none of the semitranslation surface strata have exactly one cone point of cone angle π\pi, no semitranslation surface stratum which can be double covered to produce a genus 3 surface satisfies the hypothesis of Theorem 2.5.

5. Blocking Sets to Oblivious Points

We provide an alternate construction that may be used to prove the main results from the previous section, generating oblivious points by branching over specific points on a square torus. This technique works in all genus g≥3g\geq 3, thereby proving Theorem 1.4, which may not be proved by the previous methods as shown.

5.1. Blocking Sets

For any surface XX and any point x∈Xx\in X, a finite set of points P={p1,…,pn}⊆XP=\{p_{1},\dots,p_{n}\}\subseteq X is called a blocking set of xx if every closed geodesic through xx contains a point in the blocking set. xx is said to be blocked by PP.

The set P={(0,12),(12,0),(12,12)}P=\{(0,\frac{1}{2}),(\frac{1}{2},0),(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2})\} is known to block the point (0,0)(0,0) on the unit square torus (see Figure 6). For a detailed discussion of blocking sets on tori, see Lelièvre, Monteil, and Weiss [5, Section 6].

Lemma 5.1.

Let XX be a translation surface with point xx and blocking set PP of xx. Suppose YY is a fully ramified branched translation cover with a translation cover ρ:Y→X\rho:Y\rightarrow X with ρ−1​(P)\rho^{-1}(P) being cone points. Then any point in ρ−1​(x)\rho^{-1}(x) is oblivious.

Proof.

Any closed geodesic through xx will contain a point in PP. Suppose y∈ρ−1​(x)y\in\rho^{-1}(x) is not oblivious. Then there is some non-singular closed geodesic γ\gamma containing yy in YY. By Lemma 3.53.5 ρ⁡(γ)\rho(\gamma) is a closed geodesic containing xx. However, this implies that ρ⁡(γ)∩P≠∅\rho(\gamma)\cap P\neq\emptyset. Thus γ∩ρ−1​(P)≠∅\gamma\cap\rho^{-1}(P)\neq\emptyset. By assumption any point in ρ−1​(P)\rho^{-1}(P) is a cone point, but γ\gamma is non-singular, a contradiction. ∎

Using the slit construction, create a translation surface YY with four cone points, each with cone angle 4​π4\pi (see Figure 7). This is achieved by identifying slits on two square tori with marked points at P={(0,1/2),(1/4,1/2),(1/2,1/2),(1/2,0)}P=\{(0,1/2),(1/4,1/2),(1/2,1/2),(1/2,0)\}. As PP is a blocking set on each torus for the point at the origin, any closed geodesic on YY containing y1y_{1} or y2y_{2} must pass through a cone point.

Now we generalise this construction to prove the main results from the previous section. We note in the lemma ρ\rho by definition is fully ramified and hence the following constructions will produce fully ramified covers.

Construction 5.2 (2 oblivious points).

Consider the square torus XX with marked points P={p1=(12,0),p2=(0,12),p3=(12,12),p4=(14,12)}P=\{p_{1}=(\frac{1}{2},0),p_{2}=(0,\frac{1}{2}),p_{3}=(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}),p_{4}=(\frac{1}{4},\frac{1}{2})\} and xx the point at the origin. Since PP contains a blocking set, xx is blocked by PP.

Now consider (Y,ρ)(Y,\rho), a translation double cover of XX branched over PP with slit identification as shown in Figure 4. The points marked with “X” are the preimages of the pip_{i} and are cone points of angle 4​π4\pi each. Since xx is blocked in (X,P)(X,P) and ρ−1​{x}={y1,y2}\rho^{-1}\{x\}=\{y_{1},y_{2}\}, Lemma 5.1 implies that y1y_{1} and y2y_{2} are both oblivious in YY.

Construction 5.3 (n oblivious points).

Consider (Z,σ:Z→X)(Z,\sigma:Z\to X), a degree nn translation cover of XX branching over PP with cyclic slit identification as shown in Figure 8.

Note that there are only 44 cone points each with angle 2​π​n2\pi n at the identified preimages of the original 44 marked points. We have ρ−1​{x}={x1,…,xn}\rho^{-1}\{x\}=\{x_{1},\dots,x_{n}\} and since xx is blocked in (X,P)(X,P), by Lemma 5.1, all the xix_{i} are oblivious in YY. By Lemma 3.1, we know that all non-oblivious points in XX have non-oblivious preimages, so our cover construction has exactly nn oblivious points.

One is finally able to prove Theorem 1.4.

Proof of Theorem 1.4.

The previous construction yields 44 cone points of angle 2​π​n2\pi n. For n=2n=2 this amounts to having angle excess 8​π8\pi which corresponds to a genus 33 surface by Gauss-Bonnet. Together with our Theorem 4.3 this proves Theorem 1.4.

In general, the construction yields a genus 2​n−12n-1 surface by Gauss-Bonnet. To obtain even genera one may take our genus 2​n−12n-1 construction and add a slit between any pair of squares from the coordinates (5/8,7/8)(5/8,7/8) to (7/8,5/8)(7/8,5/8). This slit adds 2 cone points with angle excess 2​π2\pi each, therefore resulting in a genus 2​n2n surface. ∎

6. Tilings and Oblivious Points

Corollary 6.1.

For every n≥4n\geq 4, there is a square tiled surface with 2​n2n tiles and exactly one oblivious point.

Proof.

If one takes the canonical double cover of the 4-square L shown above, one gets an 8-square STS with one oblivious point by Theorem 2.5 and Lemma 2.6 (the conditions of Lemma 2.6 are met with Lemma 3.3 because all vertex points are one cone point). One may add a square to this base L to get a 5-tiled L which becomes a 10-square STS with an oblivious point (the conditions of Lemma 2.6 are still met because only one vertex point, AA, has been added and it is contained within the simple closed geodesic that is the vertical line shown). If one continues to add squares in this manner, one can get an even-tiled STS with an oblivious point for any even number greater than or equal to 8. ∎

Lemma 6.2.

There is no square-tiled surface with two or four tiles and an oblivious point

Proof.

Proposition 19 of Matheus [6] states that a square tiled surface in ℋ⁡(k1,…,kn)\mathcal{H}(k_{1},\dots,k_{n}) is tiled by at least N=∑i=1n(kn+1)N=\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}(k_{n}+1) squares.

Hence, every two tiled surface is in ℋ⁡(0)\mathcal{H}(0), i.e. has genus 1. Every four tiled surface is in ℋ⁡(0),ℋ⁡(1,1)\mathcal{H}(0),\mathcal{H}(1,1) or ℋ⁡(2)\mathcal{H}(2) i.e. has genus 1 or 2. By Proposition 4.4 there is no oblivious point on any surface of genus 1 or 2, hence no two or four tiled STS has an oblivious point. ∎

Remark 6.3.

For the same reason as Lemma 6.2 every six tiled surface is in one of the following strata: ℋ⁡(0),ℋ⁡(1,1),ℋ⁡(2),ℋ⁡(2,2),ℋ⁡(1,3),ℋ⁡(4)\mathcal{H}(0),\mathcal{H}(1,1),\mathcal{H}(2),\mathcal{H}(2,2),\mathcal{H}(1,3),\mathcal{H}(4), all of which have genus ⩽3\leqslant 3. However, by Proposition 4.4 no surface of genus 1 or 2 has an oblivious point on it, hence if such a surface exists, it must be in one of the following strata: ℋ⁡(4),ℋ⁡(1,3)\mathcal{H}(4),\mathcal{H}(1,3) or ℋ⁡(2,2)\mathcal{H}(2,2). No surface with an oblivious point in any of these strata (and consequently with six tiles) can be obtained through Proposition 2.5, however, the existence of such a surface in general is unknown.

Corollary 6.4.

For every odd integer m=k​n2,k≥3,n≥3,m=kn^{2},k\geq 3,n\geq 3, there exists a square tiled surface with mm tiles and exactly kk oblivious points on it.

Proof.

To construct such a surface, one generalises the slit construction from Section 5. On the unit square torus one marks all the points at coordinates (pn,qn),p,q∈{1,2,…,n}\displaystyle\quantity(\frac{p}{n}, \frac qn),p,q\in\quantity{1, 2, \dots, n}. By Lelièvre, Monteil, and Weiss [5, Section 6], tbis set constitutes a blocking set for the origin.

Hence, by taking a kk–cover of this surface and slitting the kk copies together as was done in Section 5, one obtains a a translation surface with exactly kk oblivious points, one at the origin of each sheet. An example of the construction with k×32k\times 3^{2} tiles is shown in Figure 10.

This construction gives one the requisite surface with k​n2kn^{2} tiles and kk oblivious points. This surface is in ℋ⁡((k−1)4​(2​n+1))\mathcal{H}((k-1)^{4(2n+1)}) and has genus 2​(2​n+1)​(k−1)+12(2n+1)(k-1)+1 ∎

Let us conclude with a final question: for large enough nn, can one always construct a STS from nn squares which has an oblivious point?

Question 6.5.

Is there an NN such that for all n≥Nn\geq N, there exists a square-tiled surface with exactly nn tiles and an oblivious point?
